The Cook Partisan Voting Index (PVI) is a measure of competitiveness in U.S. congressional districts based on the methodology introduced by Rob Richie of the Center for Voting and Democracy (now FairVote). The index looks at how every congressional district voted in the past two presidential elections combined and compares it to the national average. The Cook PVI is displayed as a letter, a plus sign, and a number, with the letter (either a D for Democratic or an R for Republican) indicating the party that won the district and the number showing how many percentage points above the national average it received.

In 2022, the formula was updated to weigh the most recent presidential election more heavily. In healthcare settings, transgender individuals may face discrimination known as "trans broken arm syndrome," in which doctors mistakenly assume that a trans person's medical ailments stem from their trans status or gender-affirming care and consequently treat their problem incorrectly or deny them care entirely. Trans patients often hide their trans status when visiting a doctor if their problem, such as a broken arm, isn't related to their trans status. This is especially common in rural or more conservative areas.

Transgender people have the right to medical privacy. According to the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), medical providers and insurance companies are prohibited from disclosing any personal medical information including a person's transgender status. HIPAA also allows transgender people to access and receive a copy of their medical records from health care facilities. Insurance coverage for gender-affirming healthcare can vary widely, and transgender individuals may face barriers to accessing necessary care.
